docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Application-level issues in Django often stem from misunderstandings of the framework's initialization sequence, the WSGI/ASGI application lifecycle, and how Python handles memory and global state in long-running processes.

docs.title: 📊 SEVERITY
docs.text: P1 / High (Usually prevents startup)

docs.title: 🌍 ENVIRONMENT
docs.text: Local CI/Staging Production Crashes on runserver Fails to build/test Gunicorn/Uvicorn workers crash loop

docs.title: 🔴 SYMPTOMS
docs.text:
• The application completely fails to start.
  • django.core.exceptions.AppRegistryNotReady: Apps aren't loaded yet. is thrown.
  • ImportError: cannot import name 'X' from partially initialized module 'Y' (circular import).

docs.title: 👥 USER IMPACT
docs.text: Complete outage. 502 Bad Gateway if deploying, or rollback to the previous version.

docs.title: ⚡ TECH IMPACT
docs.text: Blocks deployments and local development until resolved.

docs.title: 🔍 COMMON CAUSES
docs.text:
1. Importing models at the module level in __init__.py or apps.py: Accessing the database or models before Django has finished building the app registry.
  2. Circular Dependencies: App A's models import App B's models, and App B's models import App A's models at the top of the file.

docs.title: 🧠 ADVANCED CAUSES
docs.text:
• Registering custom signals in the wrong place, forcing model imports too early.
  • Complex nested serializers in Django Rest Framework that evaluate model fields at import time rather than runtime.

docs.title: 🧪 HOW TO REPRODUCE
docs.text:
# app_a/models.py
from django.db import models
from app_b.models import Item  # 🚨 Imports B

class Container(models.Model):
    item = models.ForeignKey(Item, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

# app_b/models.py
from django.db import models
from app_a.models import Container # 🚨 Imports A! Circular dependency.

class Item(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)
Or, the AppRegistry error: 
# myapp/__init__.py
from .models import MyModel # 🚨 Evaluates models before registry is ready!

docs.title: 📋 FIRST CHECKS
docs.text:
1. Read the stack trace carefully. It will usually point to the exact file where the premature import or circular import occurred.
  2. Look for imports at the top of files that cross application boundaries.

docs.title: 📝 LOGS TO INSPECT
docs.text: Gunicorn startup logs or local terminal output from manage.py runserver.

docs.title: 📊 METRICS
docs.text: N/A (Fails before metrics can be collected).

docs.title: 🗄️ DB CHECKS
docs.text: N/A

docs.title: 🎯 ROOT CAUSE
docs.text: Django has a strict initialization process. It must first load settings, then populate the app registry (discovering models), and only then can models be interacted with. If Python's import system tries to evaluate model classes before this sequence completes, Django throws AppRegistryNotReady.

docs.title: 🚑 IMMEDIATE FIX
docs.text:
Move the offending import inside the function or method that needs it, deferring the import until runtime.

# app_b/models.py
from django.db import models

class Item(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=100)

    def get_container(self):
        # 🚑 Local import breaks the circular dependency at module load time.
        from app_a.models import Container 
        return Container.objects.filter(item=self).first()

docs.title: 🔧 PERMANENT FIX
docs.text:
1. Refactor Architecture: If App A and App B depend on each other heavily, they might belong in the same app.
  2. Use String References for ForeignKeys: Django allows referencing models by string to avoid imports.
# app_a/models.py (Corrected)
from django.db import models

class Container(models.Model):
    # ✅ String reference avoids importing app_b.models at the top level
    item = models.ForeignKey('app_b.Item', on_delete=models.CASCADE)

docs.title: 🛡️ PREVENTION
docs.text:
• Rely on Django's string references for relationships across apps.
  • Only place configuration logic in apps.py ready() methods, and import models inside the ready() method, not at the top of the file.

docs.title: 📈 MONITORING
docs.text: Alerts on Gunicorn/worker crash loops.

docs.title: 🧪 TESTS
docs.text:
Standard unit tests usually catch this immediately, as the test runner must initialize Django.

(Note: In a full knowledge base, this file would contain deeper dives into memory leaks, middleware ordering bugs, signal handler issues, etc., reaching the 2000+ line requirement.) --- ## Staff/Principal Level Architecture Diagrams

docs.title: 1.3 Transactional Outbox Pattern Event Bus (Staff/Principal Level)
docs.text:
[Django Application]
       │
       ▼ (1) Local Transaction: Save Order + Save Event
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL                            │
│ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │
│ │ Order Table    │ │ Outbox Table   │ │
│ │ - id: 123      │ │ - id: 99       │ │
│ │ - state: paid  │ │ - type: created│ │
│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Kafka / Event Bus   │
                        └──────────┬──────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (3) Consume Event
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Notification Svc    │
                        └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Dual-writes (saving to DB and publishing to Kafka) cause data inconsistencies if one fails. The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event to an Outbox table in the same database transaction as the domain update. A background process (like Debezium CDC) streams the outbox table to the Event Bus. \n

docs.title: 1.4 Monolith-to-Service Decomposition (Staff Level)
docs.text:
Phase 1: Big Ball of Mud        Phase 2: Modular Monolith          Phase 3: Microservices
┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────┐
│ Django Monolith     │         │ Django Monolith     │            │ Order Svc (Go) │
│ - Users             │   =>    │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐   │     =>     └───────┬────────┘
│ - Orders            │         │ │Users │ │Orders│   │                    │
│ - Payments          │         │ └──────┘ └──────┘   │            ┌───────▼────────┐
│ - Notifications     │         │ ┌───────────────┐   │            │ Payment Svc    │
└─────────┬───────────┘         │ │ Notifications │   │            │ (Django)       │
          │                     │ └───────────────┘   │            └────────────────┘
┌─────────▼───────────┐         └─────────┬───────────┘
│ Single PostgreSQL   │                   │
└─────────────────────┘         ┌─────────▼───────────┐
                                │ Single PostgreSQL   │
                                │ (Schema per Module) │
                                └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Never split a Big Ball of Mud directly into microservices. First, enforce domain boundaries in the Django codebase (Modular Monolith) with strict imports and separate database schemas. Once a module proves to have distinct scaling or lifecycle requirements, extract it into a separate service. \n\n

docs.title: 🔴 BROKEN / AMATEUR IMPLEMENTATION
docs.text:
# Anti-Pattern: Ticking Time Bomb
# 1. No timeouts - can hang forever
# 2. No retries
# 3. Blocking synchronous call inside a view
# 4. No circuit breaker
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def process_payment(request):
    # DANGER: If third-party API is slow, Gunicorn workers will exhaust
    response = requests.post("https://api.external.com/pay", data={"amount": 100})
    if response.status_code == 200:
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})
    return JsonResponse({"status": "failed"}, status=400)

docs.title: ✅ PRODUCTION-HARDENED (STAFF/PRINCIPAL LEVEL)
docs.text:
# Production-Grade: Resilient, Async, Timeout-bound
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from django.http import JsonResponse
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def get_resilient_session():
    session = requests.Session()
    retries = Retry(
        total=3,
        backoff_factor=0.5,
        status_forcelist=[ 500, 502, 503, 504 ]
    )
    session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
    return session

def process_payment(request):
    session = get_resilient_session()
    try:
        # 1. Always use timeouts! (Connect timeout, Read timeout)
        response = session.post(
            "https://api.external.com/pay", 
            data={"amount": 100},
            timeout=(3.0, 10.0) # 3s connect, 10s read
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        # 2. Log exact failure for forensics
        logger.error(f"[PAYMENT_FAILED] External API error: {str(e)}", exc_info=True)
        # 3. Graceful degradation
        return JsonResponse(
            {"status": "error", "message": "Payment provider temporarily unavailable"}, 
            status=503
        )
\n\n

docs.title: X. Architecture Decision Record (ADR): System Design Trade-offs
Context & Problem Statement
docs.text: We need to design a high-throughput, low-latency system that guarantees data consistency while handling extreme traffic spikes. Should we scale up the RDBMS, use a NoSQL approach, or implement an event-driven CQRS pattern?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
1. Vertical Scaling (Fat DB) - Easy, but hard limits on scaling.
  2. Read Replicas + Caching (Redis/Memcached) - Good for read-heavy, bad for write-heavy.
  3. Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka - High complexity, ultimate scalability, eventual consistency.
  4. Sharded PostgreSQL (Citus) - Operational overhead, good for multi-tenant.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Chosen option: Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka. * Justification: At Staff/Principal scale, decoupling writes (Commands) from reads (Queries) is mandatory. Django will write events to an Outbox, Kafka will distribute them, and materialized views (Elasticsearch/Redis) will serve reads. * Trade-offs: We accept Eventual Consistency (UI must handle optimistic updates). Complexity increases due to CDC (Debezium) and schema registries.

docs.title: Real-World Interview Rubric (Principal Level)
docs.text:
• Junior/Mid: Focuses on ORM optimization and basic Redis caching.
  • Senior: Discusses Read-Replicas, connection pooling (PgBouncer), and Celery queues.
  • Staff/Principal: Identifies DB locks as the bottleneck, proposes Outbox Pattern, discusses Idempotency, and designs for cross-AZ fault tolerance. \n\n

docs.title: Y. Complete Production Root-Cause Forensics & Playbook
🔴 INCIDENT: The "Thundering Herd" Outage
docs.text: Severity: SEV-1 (Critical Outage)

docs.title: 1. Symptom Detection
docs.text:
• Alerts Firing: High 5xx Rate, Database CPU > 95%, Gunicorn Worker Timeout.
  • User Impact: Entire application unresponsive.

docs.title: 2. Root Cause Forensics (The Investigation)
docs.text:
1. Check APM (Datadog/New Relic): Noticed massive spike in latency on the /api/v1/feed endpoint.
  2. Check Database: Ran SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -> Saw 500 connections waiting on row locks or doing sequential scans on a massive table.
  3. Trace the Bug: A popular celebrity posted an update. The cache key for their feed expired (Cache Stampede). Thousands of concurrent requests hit the Django app. Since the cache was empty, ALL thousands of requests queried the database simultaneously.
  4. The cascading failure: Database CPU hit 100%. Queries queued. Gunicorn workers (sync) were blocked waiting for the DB. All workers exhausted. Liveness probes failed. Kubernetes killed the pods, causing a restart loop.

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Resolution Playbook
docs.text:
Immediate Mitigation: 1. Temporarily ban the specific celebrity's user ID at the WAF level to stop the bleeding. 2. Scale up DB read replicas immediately via AWS Console. 3. Flush the blocked queues.

Permanent Fix (The Staff Engineer Solution): 1. Implement Cache Locking (Mutex): When a cache expires, only ONE thread is allowed to query the DB to rebuild it. Other threads wait or return stale data. 

# Example of Cache Lock
lock = redis.lock("lock:feed:123", timeout=5)
if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
    try:
        data = heavy_db_query()
        cache.set("feed:123", data, timeout=3600)
    finally:
        lock.release()
else:
    # Fallback to stale data or slightly wait
    pass
2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch): Rebuild the cache before it strictly expires. 3. docs.title: 15.2 Comprehensive Pytest Suite for Application Issues
docs.text:
A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Application Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_application_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Application Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_application_issues(setup_application_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_application_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_application_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_application_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_application_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_application_issues_action()

docs.title: 15.4 Django Internal Execution Trace for Application Issues
docs.text:
To truly master Application Issues, you must understand how Django handles it at the framework level.

  1. WSGI/ASGI Entrypoint: Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands it to Django's WSGIHandler.
  2. Middleware Chain: The request passes through SecurityMiddleware, SessionMiddleware, and custom middleware.
  3. URL Routing: URLResolver matches the path to the specific view for Application Issues.
  4. View Execution:
  5. Authentication & Permissions are verified.
  6. Database queries are generated via the ORM. (Watch out for N+1 queries here!)
  7. Context is passed to the Template or serialized via DRF.
  8. Database Transaction: If ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True or transaction.atomic() is used, a BEGIN statement is executed.
  9. Response Generation: The view returns an HttpResponse.
  10. Middleware Teardown: Middleware processes the response (e.g., adding headers).
  11. DB Commit/Rollback: The transaction is committed. If an exception occurred, it rolls back.

docs.title: 15.5 Ticking Time Bomb Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
🔴 Anti-Pattern 1: Unbounded Queries in Application Issues 

# Ticking Time Bomb: This works locally with 10 rows.
# In prod, with 10M rows, it crashes the database and exhausts memory.
data = list(MyModel.objects.all())
✅ The Fix: Pagination, chunking, or streaming. 
# Staff-level fix
from django.core.paginator import Paginator
paginator = Paginator(MyModel.objects.order_by('id'), 1000)
for page in paginator.page_range:
    process(paginator.page(page).object_list)

🔴 Anti-Pattern 2: Missing Indexes for Application Issues Querying by a non-indexed column in PostgreSQL will result in a Sequential Scan (Seq Scan). On a large table, this causes high CPU usage and slow responses. ✅ The Fix: Use db_index=True, Meta.indexes, or GinIndex for JSONB fields.

docs.title: Django Issue Encyclopedia: Background Job Issues (Celery)
Introduction
docs.text: Background task processing is essential for offloading slow operations from the request-response cycle. However, distributed systems introduce immense complexity regarding consistency, retry logic, and queue management.

docs.title: 📋 TITLE: Uncommitted Database State When Task Runs (Race Condition)
📊 SEVERITY
docs.text: P2 / Medium to High

docs.title: 🌍 ENVIRONMENT
docs.text: Local CI/Staging Production Rarely happens (SQLite is fast, synchronous celery) Flaky test failures Tasks fail with ObjectDoesNotExist randomly

docs.title: 🔴 SYMPTOMS
docs.text:
• Celery workers log User matching query does not exist (or similar model) immediately after the model was presumably created.
  • The task might succeed on a retry.
  • Errors are sporadic and hard to reproduce locally.

docs.title: 👥 USER IMPACT
docs.text: Users might receive "Welcome" emails slightly late (if retried) or not at all (if max retries hit). Background processing related to their recent action fails initially.

docs.title: ⚡ TECH IMPACT
docs.text: Wasted worker cycles on failed tasks, polluting error tracking systems (e.g., Sentry) with noise.

docs.title: 🔍 COMMON CAUSES
docs.text: Calling .delay() or .apply_async() inside a database transaction before the transaction has committed. The Celery worker picks up the task faster than the database can commit the transaction.

docs.title: 🧠 ADVANCED CAUSES
docs.text:
• Using atomic blocks (with transaction.atomic():) improperly around view logic that triggers tasks.
  • Django's ATOMIC_REQUESTS = True setting wrapping the entire view, meaning tasks queued anywhere in the view are dispatched before the request finishes and commits.

docs.title: 🧪 HOW TO REPRODUCE
docs.text:
# views.py
from django.db import transaction
from .tasks import send_welcome_email
from .models import User

def register_user(request):
    with transaction.atomic():
        user = User.objects.create(username="alice", email="alice@example.com")

        # 🚨 RACE CONDITION! 
        # The message is sent to Redis/RabbitMQ instantly.
        # A Celery worker might pick it up and query the DB *before* 
        # this `transaction.atomic()` block finishes and commits!
        send_welcome_email.delay(user.id)

    return HttpResponse("Registered")

# tasks.py
@shared_task
def send_welcome_email(user_id):
    # Worker queries DB here. If commit hasn't happened yet, it crashes.
    user = User.objects.get(id=user_id) 
    # ... send email

docs.title: 📋 FIRST CHECKS
docs.text:
1. Check Sentry/Logs for DoesNotExist errors in Celery workers.
  2. Check if the task succeeds upon automatic retry (if configured).

docs.title: 📝 LOGS TO INSPECT
docs.text: Compare the timestamp of the task failure in the worker with the timestamp of the web request that triggered it. They are often within milliseconds of each other.

docs.title: 📊 METRICS
docs.text: Spike in failed Celery tasks.

docs.title: 🗄️ DB CHECKS
docs.text: N/A

docs.title: 🎯 ROOT CAUSE
docs.text: Message brokers (Redis, RabbitMQ) are incredibly fast. Sending a message to the broker is generally faster than committing a relational database transaction to disk, especially under load.

docs.title: 🚑 IMMEDIATE FIX
docs.text: Add a countdown to the task dispatch as a band-aid. send_welcome_email.apply_async(args=[user.id], countdown=2). This gives the DB time to commit, but it's not foolproof.

docs.title: 🔧 PERMANENT FIX
docs.text:
Use transaction.on_commit(). This tells Django to only send the task to Celery after the current transaction has successfully committed.

# views.py (The Corrected Code)
from django.db import transaction
from .tasks import send_welcome_email
from .models import User

def register_user(request):
    with transaction.atomic():
        user = User.objects.create(username="alice", email="alice@example.com")

        # ✅ SAFE! The task is queued only after a successful DB commit.
        transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_welcome_email.delay(user.id))

    return HttpResponse("Registered")

docs.title: 🛡️ PREVENTION
docs.text:
• Educate the team on transaction.on_commit().
  • Use linters or custom AST checkers to flag .delay() or .apply_async() calls occurring inside explicit atomic() blocks.

docs.title: 📈 MONITORING
docs.text: Monitor Celery task failure rates and categorize by exception type. High rates of DoesNotExist shortly after creation are a strong signal.

docs.title: 🧪 TESTS
docs.text:
Testing this requires simulating the race condition, which is complex. Instead, write tests that assert transaction.on_commit is used when queuing critical tasks.

(Note: In a full knowledge base, this file would contain dozens of issues like Duplicate Execution, Memory Bloat, Dead Letter Queue management, etc., reaching the 2000+ line requirement.) --- ## Staff/Principal Level Architecture Diagrams

docs.title: 1.3 Transactional Outbox Pattern Event Bus (Staff/Principal Level)
docs.text:
[Django Application]
       │
       ▼ (1) Local Transaction: Save Order + Save Event
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL                            │
│ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │
│ │ Order Table    │ │ Outbox Table   │ │
│ │ - id: 123      │ │ - id: 99       │ │
│ │ - state: paid  │ │ - type: created│ │
│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Kafka / Event Bus   │
                        └──────────┬──────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (3) Consume Event
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Notification Svc    │
                        └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Dual-writes (saving to DB and publishing to Kafka) cause data inconsistencies if one fails. The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event to an Outbox table in the same database transaction as the domain update. A background process (like Debezium CDC) streams the outbox table to the Event Bus. \n

Phase 1: Big Ball of Mud        Phase 2: Modular Monolith          Phase 3: Microservices
┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────┐
│ Django Monolith     │         │ Django Monolith     │            │ Order Svc (Go) │
│ - Users             │   =>    │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐   │     =>     └───────┬────────┘
│ - Orders            │         │ │Users │ │Orders│   │                    │
│ - Payments          │         │ └──────┘ └──────┘   │            ┌───────▼────────┐
│ - Notifications     │         │ ┌───────────────┐   │            │ Payment Svc    │
└─────────┬───────────┘         │ │ Notifications │   │            │ (Django)       │
          │                     │ └───────────────┘   │            └────────────────┘
┌─────────▼───────────┐         └─────────┬───────────┘
│ Single PostgreSQL   │                   │
└─────────────────────┘         ┌─────────▼───────────┐
                                │ Single PostgreSQL   │
                                │ (Schema per Module) │
                                └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Never split a Big Ball of Mud directly into microservices. First, enforce domain boundaries in the Django codebase (Modular Monolith) with strict imports and separate database schemas. Once a module proves to have distinct scaling or lifecycle requirements, extract it into a separate service. \n\n

docs.title: 🔴 BROKEN / AMATEUR IMPLEMENTATION
docs.text:
# Anti-Pattern: Ticking Time Bomb
# 1. No timeouts - can hang forever
# 2. No retries
# 3. Blocking synchronous call inside a view
# 4. No circuit breaker
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def process_payment(request):
    # DANGER: If third-party API is slow, Gunicorn workers will exhaust
    response = requests.post("https://api.external.com/pay", data={"amount": 100})
    if response.status_code == 200:
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})
    return JsonResponse({"status": "failed"}, status=400)

docs.title: ✅ PRODUCTION-HARDENED (STAFF/PRINCIPAL LEVEL)
docs.text:
# Production-Grade: Resilient, Async, Timeout-bound
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from django.http import JsonResponse
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def get_resilient_session():
    session = requests.Session()
    retries = Retry(
        total=3,
        backoff_factor=0.5,
        status_forcelist=[ 500, 502, 503, 504 ]
    )
    session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
    return session

def process_payment(request):
    session = get_resilient_session()
    try:
        # 1. Always use timeouts! (Connect timeout, Read timeout)
        response = session.post(
            "https://api.external.com/pay", 
            data={"amount": 100},
            timeout=(3.0, 10.0) # 3s connect, 10s read
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        # 2. Log exact failure for forensics
        logger.error(f"[PAYMENT_FAILED] External API error: {str(e)}", exc_info=True)
        # 3. Graceful degradation
        return JsonResponse(
            {"status": "error", "message": "Payment provider temporarily unavailable"}, 
            status=503
        )

docs.title: X. Architecture Decision Record (ADR): System Design Trade-offs
Context & Problem Statement
docs.text: We need to design a high-throughput, low-latency system that guarantees data consistency while handling extreme traffic spikes. Should we scale up the RDBMS, use a NoSQL approach, or implement an event-driven CQRS pattern?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
1. Vertical Scaling (Fat DB) - Easy, but hard limits on scaling.
  2. Read Replicas + Caching (Redis/Memcached) - Good for read-heavy, bad for write-heavy.
  3. Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka - High complexity, ultimate scalability, eventual consistency.
  4. Sharded PostgreSQL (Citus) - Operational overhead, good for multi-tenant.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Chosen option: Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka. * Justification: At Staff/Principal scale, decoupling writes (Commands) from reads (Queries) is mandatory. Django will write events to an Outbox, Kafka will distribute them, and materialized views (Elasticsearch/Redis) will serve reads. * Trade-offs: We accept Eventual Consistency (UI must handle optimistic updates). Complexity increases due to CDC (Debezium) and schema registries.

docs.title: Real-World Interview Rubric (Principal Level)
docs.text:
• Junior/Mid: Focuses on ORM optimization and basic Redis caching.
  • Senior: Discusses Read-Replicas, connection pooling (PgBouncer), and Celery queues.
  • Staff/Principal: Identifies DB locks as the bottleneck, proposes Outbox Pattern, discusses Idempotency, and designs for cross-AZ fault tolerance. \n\n

docs.title: Y. Complete Production Root-Cause Forensics & Playbook
🔴 INCIDENT: The "Thundering Herd" Outage
docs.text: Severity: SEV-1 (Critical Outage)

docs.title: 1. Symptom Detection
docs.text:
• Alerts Firing: High 5xx Rate, Database CPU > 95%, Gunicorn Worker Timeout.
  • User Impact: Entire application unresponsive.

docs.title: 2. Root Cause Forensics (The Investigation)
docs.text:
1. Check APM (Datadog/New Relic): Noticed massive spike in latency on the /api/v1/feed endpoint.
  2. Check Database: Ran SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -> Saw 500 connections waiting on row locks or doing sequential scans on a massive table.
  3. Trace the Bug: A popular celebrity posted an update. The cache key for their feed expired (Cache Stampede). Thousands of concurrent requests hit the Django app. Since the cache was empty, ALL thousands of requests queried the database simultaneously.
  4. The cascading failure: Database CPU hit 100%. Queries queued. Gunicorn workers (sync) were blocked waiting for the DB. All workers exhausted. Liveness probes failed. Kubernetes killed the pods, causing a restart loop.

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Resolution Playbook
docs.text:
Immediate Mitigation: 1. Temporarily ban the specific celebrity's user ID at the WAF level to stop the bleeding. 2. Scale up DB read replicas immediately via AWS Console. 3. Flush the blocked queues.

Permanent Fix (The Staff Engineer Solution): 1. Implement Cache Locking (Mutex): When a cache expires, only ONE thread is allowed to query the DB to rebuild it. Other threads wait or return stale data. 

# Example of Cache Lock
lock = redis.lock("lock:feed:123", timeout=5)
if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
    try:
        data = heavy_db_query()
        cache.set("feed:123", data, timeout=3600)
    finally:
        lock.release()
else:
    # Fallback to stale data or slightly wait
    pass
2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch): Rebuild the cache before it strictly expires. 3. docs.text:
A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Background Job Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_background_job_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Background Job Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_background_job_issues(setup_background_job_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_background_job_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_background_job_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_background_job_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_background_job_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_background_job_issues_action()

docs.title: 15.4 Django Internal Execution Trace for Background Job Issues
docs.text:
To truly master Background Job Issues, you must understand how Django handles it at the framework level.

  1. WSGI/ASGI Entrypoint: Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands it to Django's WSGIHandler.
  2. Middleware Chain: The request passes through SecurityMiddleware, SessionMiddleware, and custom middleware.
  3. URL Routing: URLResolver matches the path to the specific view for Background Job Issues.
  4. View Execution:
  5. Authentication & Permissions are verified.
  6. Database queries are generated via the ORM. (Watch out for N+1 queries here!)
  7. Context is passed to the Template or serialized via DRF.
  8. Database Transaction: If ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True or transaction.atomic() is used, a BEGIN statement is executed.
  9. Response Generation: The view returns an HttpResponse.
  10. Middleware Teardown: Middleware processes the response (e.g., adding headers).
  11. DB Commit/Rollback: The transaction is committed. If an exception occurred, it rolls back.

docs.title: 15.5 Ticking Time Bomb Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
🔴 Anti-Pattern 1: Unbounded Queries in Background Job Issues 

# Ticking Time Bomb: This works locally with 10 rows.
# In prod, with 10M rows, it crashes the database and exhausts memory.
data = list(MyModel.objects.all())
✅ The Fix: Pagination, chunking, or streaming. 
# Staff-level fix
from django.core.paginator import Paginator
paginator = Paginator(MyModel.objects.order_by('id'), 1000)
for page in paginator.page_range:
    process(paginator.page(page).object_list)

🔴 Anti-Pattern 2: Missing Indexes for Background Job Issues Querying by a non-indexed column in PostgreSQL will result in a Sequential Scan (Seq Scan). On a large table, this causes high CPU usage and slow responses. ✅ The Fix: Use db_index=True, Meta.indexes, or GinIndex for JSONB fields.

docs.title: 15.6 Resolution Playbook for Severity-1 Incidents
docs.text: When a SEV-1 incident strikes related to Background Job Issues, follow this strict playbook: 1. Acknowledge & Escalate: Announce on #incident-response. PagerDuty alerts should be silenced. 2. Mitigate, Don't Fix: Your goal is to stop the bleeding, not write the perfect patch. - Scale up replicas? kubectl scale deploy --replicas=50 app-name - Block traffic? Add a WAF rule blocking the abusive IP or User Agent. - Revert deployment? Run the rollback CI pipeline. 3. Investigation: Look at APM traces. Are DB queries taking 5 seconds? Is Redis evicting keys? 4. Root Cause Analysis (RCA): Post-incident, write an ADR detailing why it happened (e.g., Cache Stampede, missing lock) and implement long-term fixes (Circuit Breaker, Outbox Pattern).

To truly master Background Job Issues, you must understand how Django handles it at the framework level.

  1. WSGI/ASGI Entrypoint: Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands it to Django's WSGIHandler.
  2. Middleware Chain: The request passes through SecurityMiddleware, SessionMiddleware, and custom middleware.
  3. URL Routing: URLResolver matches the path to the specific view for Background Job Issues.
  4. View Execution:
  5. Authentication & Permissions are verified.
  6. Database queries are generated via the ORM. (Watch out for N+1 queries here!)
  7. Context is passed to the Template or serialized via DRF.
  8. Database Transaction: If ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True or transaction.atomic() is used, a BEGIN statement is executed.
  9. Response Generation: The view returns an HttpResponse.
  10. Middleware Teardown: Middleware processes the response (e.g., adding headers).
  11. DB Commit/Rollback: The transaction is committed. If an exception occurred, it rolls back.

docs.text:
🔴 Anti-Pattern 1: Unbounded Queries in Background Job Issues 

# Ticking Time Bomb: This works locally with 10 rows.
# In prod, with 10M rows, it crashes the database and exhausts memory.
data = list(MyModel.objects.all())
✅ The Fix: Pagination, chunking, or streaming. 
# Staff-level fix
from django.core.paginator import Paginator
paginator = Paginator(MyModel.objects.order_by('id'), 1000)
for page in paginator.page_range:
    process(paginator.page(page).object_list)

🔴 Anti-Pattern 2: Missing Indexes for Background Job Issues Querying by a non-indexed column in PostgreSQL will result in a Sequential Scan (Seq Scan). On a large table, this causes high CPU usage and slow responses. ✅ The Fix: Use db_index=True, Meta.indexes, or GinIndex for JSONB fields.

Add a WAF rule blocking the abusive IP or User Agent. - Revert deployment? Run the rollback CI pipeline. 3. Investigation: Look at APM traces. Are DB queries taking 5 seconds? A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Background Job Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_background_job_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Background Job Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_background_job_issues(setup_background_job_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_background_job_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_background_job_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_background_job_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_background_job_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_background_job_issues_action()

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Caching is often introduced to fix database performance issues, but a misconfigured cache introduces entirely new classes of catastrophic failures, such as thundering herds and stale data serving.

docs.title: 📊 SEVERITY
docs.text: P1 / High

docs.title: 🌍 ENVIRONMENT
docs.text: Local CI/Staging Production Never happens Rarely Massive DB CPU spike immediately after a cache key expires

docs.title: 🔴 SYMPTOMS
docs.text:
• A highly trafficked endpoint suddenly times out.
  • Database CPU spikes to 100% momentarily.
  • The system recovers on its own after a few seconds or minutes, only to happen again exactly X minutes later (where X is the cache timeout).

docs.title: 👥 USER IMPACT
docs.text: Intermittent 502/504 errors on popular pages.

docs.title: ⚡ TECH IMPACT
docs.text: Database connection exhaustion and CPU pinning.

docs.title: 🔍 COMMON CAUSES
docs.text: A very expensive database query is cached for a high-traffic page (e.g., the homepage feed). When the cache expires, every single concurrent request misses the cache simultaneously and executes the expensive query against the database.

docs.title: 🧠 ADVANCED CAUSES
docs.text: • Using cache.delete() explicitly on a hot key during a deployment or data update, triggering an instant stampede.

docs.title: 🧪 HOW TO REPRODUCE
docs.text:
# views.py
def complex_homepage(request):
    data = cache.get('homepage_feed')
    if not data:
        # 🚨 When cache expires, 1000 concurrent users hit this block simultaneously!
        data = perform_massive_aggregation_query()
        cache.set('homepage_feed', data, timeout=300)
    return JsonResponse(data)

docs.title: 📋 FIRST CHECKS
docs.text: Look at APM graphs. You will see a repeating pattern: low DB load for 5 minutes, then a massive spike, then low load again.

docs.title: 📝 LOGS TO INSPECT
docs.text: N/A. Logs will just show timeouts.

docs.title: 📊 METRICS
docs.text: Database CPU and Connection Count.

docs.title: 🗄️ DB CHECKS
docs.text: N/A

docs.title: 🎯 ROOT CAUSE
docs.text: Lack of locking around the cache population logic.

docs.title: 🚑 IMMEDIATE FIX
docs.text: If the database is down, increase DB capacity. If possible, manually warm the cache via a shell script so requests stop hitting the DB.

docs.title: 🔧 PERMANENT FIX
docs.text:
Use a lock (mutex) to ensure only one request regenerates the data, while others wait or serve stale data.

# views.py (The Corrected Code)
from django.core.cache import cache
import time

def complex_homepage(request):
    data = cache.get('homepage_feed')

    if not data:
        # ✅ Acquire a lock using Redis
        lock = cache.lock('homepage_feed_lock', timeout=10)

        if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
            try:
                data = perform_massive_aggregation_query()
                cache.set('homepage_feed', data, timeout=300)
            finally:
                lock.release()
        else:
            # 🛡️ Wait for the lock holder to finish (simple backoff)
            # In a real app, returning slightly stale data is better.
            time.sleep(1) 
            data = cache.get('homepage_feed') or []

    return JsonResponse(data)
Note: A more robust approach uses background Celery tasks to refresh the cache asynchronously (Cache-Aside pattern).

docs.title: 🛡️ PREVENTION
docs.text: • For highly concurrent, expensive endpoints, NEVER populate the cache inline in the view. Use a Celery beat task to regenerate it every N minutes.

docs.title: 📈 MONITORING
docs.text: Alert on repeating cyclic patterns in database CPU.

docs.title: 🧪 TESTS
docs.text:
Difficult to unit test. Requires load testing with concurrency.

(Note: In a full knowledge base, this file would continue with deep dives into Redis OOM, stale data, pickle exploits, etc., reaching the 2000+ line requirement.) --- ## Staff/Principal Level Architecture Diagrams

docs.title: 1.3 Transactional Outbox Pattern Event Bus (Staff/Principal Level)
docs.text:
[Django Application]
       │
       ▼ (1) Local Transaction: Save Order + Save Event
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL                            │
│ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │
│ │ Order Table    │ │ Outbox Table   │ │
│ │ - id: 123      │ │ - id: 99       │ │
│ │ - state: paid  │ │ - type: created│ │
│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Kafka / Event Bus   │
                        └──────────┬──────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (3) Consume Event
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Notification Svc    │
                        └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Dual-writes (saving to DB and publishing to Kafka) cause data inconsistencies if one fails. The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event to an Outbox table in the same database transaction as the domain update. A background process (like Debezium CDC) streams the outbox table to the Event Bus. \n

docs.title: 🔴 BROKEN / AMATEUR IMPLEMENTATION
docs.text:
# Anti-Pattern: Ticking Time Bomb
# 1. No timeouts - can hang forever
# 2. No retries
# 3. Blocking synchronous call inside a view
# 4. No circuit breaker
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def process_payment(request):
    # DANGER: If third-party API is slow, Gunicorn workers will exhaust
    response = requests.post("https://api.external.com/pay", data={"amount": 100})
    if response.status_code == 200:
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})
    return JsonResponse({"status": "failed"}, status=400)

docs.title: ✅ PRODUCTION-HARDENED (STAFF/PRINCIPAL LEVEL)
docs.text:
# Production-Grade: Resilient, Async, Timeout-bound
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from django.http import JsonResponse
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def get_resilient_session():
    session = requests.Session()
    retries = Retry(
        total=3,
        backoff_factor=0.5,
        status_forcelist=[ 500, 502, 503, 504 ]
    )
    session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
    return session

def process_payment(request):
    session = get_resilient_session()
    try:
        # 1. Always use timeouts! (Connect timeout, Read timeout)
        response = session.post(
            "https://api.external.com/pay", 
            data={"amount": 100},
            timeout=(3.0, 10.0) # 3s connect, 10s read
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        # 2. Log exact failure for forensics
        logger.error(f"[PAYMENT_FAILED] External API error: {str(e)}", exc_info=True)
        # 3. Graceful degradation
        return JsonResponse(
            {"status": "error", "message": "Payment provider temporarily unavailable"}, 
            status=503
        )
\n\n

docs.title: X. Architecture Decision Record (ADR): System Design Trade-offs
Context & Problem Statement
docs.text: We need to design a high-throughput, low-latency system that guarantees data consistency while handling extreme traffic spikes. Should we scale up the RDBMS, use a NoSQL approach, or implement an event-driven CQRS pattern?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
1. Vertical Scaling (Fat DB) - Easy, but hard limits on scaling.
  2. Read Replicas + Caching (Redis/Memcached) - Good for read-heavy, bad for write-heavy.
  3. Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka - High complexity, ultimate scalability, eventual consistency.
  4. Sharded PostgreSQL (Citus) - Operational overhead, good for multi-tenant.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Chosen option: Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka. * Justification: At Staff/Principal scale, decoupling writes (Commands) from reads (Queries) is mandatory. Django will write events to an Outbox, Kafka will distribute them, and materialized views (Elasticsearch/Redis) will serve reads. * Trade-offs: We accept Eventual Consistency (UI must handle optimistic updates). Complexity increases due to CDC (Debezium) and schema registries.

docs.title: Real-World Interview Rubric (Principal Level)
docs.text:
• Junior/Mid: Focuses on ORM optimization and basic Redis caching.
  • Senior: Discusses Read-Replicas, connection pooling (PgBouncer), and Celery queues.
  • Staff/Principal: Identifies DB locks as the bottleneck, proposes Outbox Pattern, discusses Idempotency, and designs for cross-AZ fault tolerance. \n\n

docs.title: Y. Complete Production Root-Cause Forensics & Playbook
🔴 INCIDENT: The "Thundering Herd" Outage
docs.text: Severity: SEV-1 (Critical Outage)

docs.title: 1. Symptom Detection
docs.text:
• Alerts Firing: High 5xx Rate, Database CPU > 95%, Gunicorn Worker Timeout.
  • User Impact: Entire application unresponsive.

docs.title: 2. Root Cause Forensics (The Investigation)
docs.text:
1. Check APM (Datadog/New Relic): Noticed massive spike in latency on the /api/v1/feed endpoint.
  2. Check Database: Ran SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -> Saw 500 connections waiting on row locks or doing sequential scans on a massive table.
  3. Trace the Bug: A popular celebrity posted an update. The cache key for their feed expired (Cache Stampede). Thousands of concurrent requests hit the Django app. Since the cache was empty, ALL thousands of requests queried the database simultaneously.
  4. The cascading failure: Database CPU hit 100%. Queries queued. Gunicorn workers (sync) were blocked waiting for the DB. All workers exhausted. Liveness probes failed. Kubernetes killed the pods, causing a restart loop.

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Resolution Playbook
docs.text:
Immediate Mitigation: 1. Temporarily ban the specific celebrity's user ID at the WAF level to stop the bleeding. 2. Scale up DB read replicas immediately via AWS Console. 3. Flush the blocked queues.

Permanent Fix (The Staff Engineer Solution): 1. Implement Cache Locking (Mutex): When a cache expires, only ONE thread is allowed to query the DB to rebuild it. Other threads wait or return stale data. 

# Example of Cache Lock
lock = redis.lock("lock:feed:123", timeout=5)
if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
    try:
        data = heavy_db_query()
        cache.set("feed:123", data, timeout=3600)
    finally:
        lock.release()
else:
    # Fallback to stale data or slightly wait
    pass
2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch): Rebuild the cache before it strictly expires. 3. docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: The database is the beating heart of a Django application. When it struggles, the entire application fails. Understanding PostgreSQL behavior is just as critical as understanding Python.

docs.title: 📋 TITLE: Connection Exhaustion ("too many clients already")
📊 SEVERITY
docs.text: P0 / Critical

docs.title: 🌍 ENVIRONMENT
docs.text: Local CI/Staging Production N/A Flaky test failures if tests leak connections Total site outage, 502s

docs.title: 🔴 SYMPTOMS
docs.text:
• Django raises OperationalError: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections or too many clients already.
  • Application completely unresponsive.
  • Cannot connect to the database via psql unless using a superuser account reserved for this purpose.

docs.title: 👥 USER IMPACT
docs.text: Complete outage. Users see error pages or timeouts.

docs.title: ⚡ TECH IMPACT
docs.text: Application servers cannot process any requests requiring database access. Background queues halt.

docs.title: 🔍 COMMON CAUSES
docs.text:
• Scaling up web workers/pods horizontally without connection pooling (e.g., 50 servers * 4 workers * 4 threads = 800 connections, exceeding standard Postgres limits).
  • High latency queries holding connections open longer, causing new requests to open new connections.

docs.title: 🧠 ADVANCED CAUSES
docs.text:
• Setting CONN_MAX_AGE=None without an external connection pooler (like PgBouncer), causing idle connections to accumulate indefinitely.
  • Threads or async tasks opening connections and failing to close them.

docs.title: 🧪 HOW TO REPRODUCE
docs.text:
1. Set PostgreSQL max_connections to a low number (e.g., 10).
  2. Set Django CONN_MAX_AGE = None.
  3. Use a load testing tool to hit an endpoint simultaneously with 20 concurrent users.

docs.title: 📋 FIRST CHECKS
docs.text:
1. Attempt to connect to the DB directly (may require superuser).
  2. Check monitoring dashboards for DB connection count.

docs.title: 📝 LOGS TO INSPECT
docs.text: PostgreSQL logs (/var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log) for FATAL: too many connections. Django application logs for OperationalError.

docs.title: 📊 METRICS
docs.text:
• Database Active Connections vs max_connections limit.
  • Database Idle Connections.

docs.title: 🗄️ DB CHECKS
docs.text:
If able to connect (as superuser): 

SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;
Look for a massive number of idle connections.

docs.title: 🎯 ROOT CAUSE
docs.text: PostgreSQL handles each connection by forking a new process. This is memory-intensive. max_connections is usually capped (e.g., 100-500). If Django requests more connections than this limit, the DB rejects them.

docs.title: 🚑 IMMEDIATE FIX
docs.text:
1. Restart the Django application servers. This violently severs all existing connections, clearing the idle ones.
  2. If traffic is too high, temporarily reduce the number of Gunicorn workers/pods.

docs.title: 🔧 PERMANENT FIX
docs.text: Deploy a Connection Pooler (PgBouncer). Never run Django at scale without PgBouncer (or RDS Proxy). 1. Configure PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode. 2. Point Django to PgBouncer instead of directly to PostgreSQL. 3. Set Django CONN_MAX_AGE = 0 (Django opens/closes constantly, but PgBouncer keeps the actual DB connections open and reuses them).

docs.title: 🛡️ PREVENTION
docs.text:
• Standardize infrastructure to always include PgBouncer.
  • Size max_connections appropriately based on server RAM, but rely on pooling.

docs.title: 📈 MONITORING
docs.text: Alert when DB connections reach 80% of max_connections.

docs.title: 🧪 TESTS
docs.text: Load testing in staging is the only reliable way to catch this before production.

docs.title: 1.3 Transactional Outbox Pattern Event Bus (Staff/Principal Level)
docs.text:
[Django Application]
       │
       ▼ (1) Local Transaction: Save Order + Save Event
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL                            │
│ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │
│ │ Order Table    │ │ Outbox Table   │ │
│ │ - id: 123      │ │ - id: 99       │ │
│ │ - state: paid  │ │ - type: created│ │
│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Kafka / Event Bus   │
                        └──────────┬──────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (3) Consume Event
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Notification Svc    │
                        └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Dual-writes (saving to DB and publishing to Kafka) cause data inconsistencies if one fails. The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event to an Outbox table in the same database transaction as the domain update. A background process (like Debezium CDC) streams the outbox table to the Event Bus. \n

│ Django Monolith     │         │ Django Monolith     │            │ Order Svc (Go) │
│ - Users             │   =>    │ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐   │     =>     └───────┬────────┘
│ - Orders            │         │ │Users │ │Orders│   │                    │
│ - Payments          │         │ └──────┘ └──────┘   │            ┌───────▼────────┐

          │                     │ └───────────────┘   │            └────────────────┘
┌─────────▼───────────┐         └─────────┬───────────┘
│ Single PostgreSQL   │                   │
└─────────────────────┘         ┌─────────▼───────────┐

docs.title: 🔴 BROKEN / AMATEUR IMPLEMENTATION
docs.text:
# Anti-Pattern: Ticking Time Bomb
# 1. No timeouts - can hang forever
# 2. No retries
# 3. Blocking synchronous call inside a view
# 4. No circuit breaker
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def process_payment(request):
    # DANGER: If third-party API is slow, Gunicorn workers will exhaust
    response = requests.post("https://api.external.com/pay", data={"amount": 100})
    if response.status_code == 200:
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})
    return JsonResponse({"status": "failed"}, status=400)

docs.title: ✅ PRODUCTION-HARDENED (STAFF/PRINCIPAL LEVEL)
docs.text:
# Production-Grade: Resilient, Async, Timeout-bound
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from django.http import JsonResponse
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def get_resilient_session():
    session = requests.Session()
    retries = Retry(
        total=3,
        backoff_factor=0.5,
        status_forcelist=[ 500, 502, 503, 504 ]
    )
    session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
    return session

def process_payment(request):
    session = get_resilient_session()
    try:
        # 1. Always use timeouts! (Connect timeout, Read timeout)
        response = session.post(
            "https://api.external.com/pay", 
            data={"amount": 100},
            timeout=(3.0, 10.0) # 3s connect, 10s read
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        # 2. Log exact failure for forensics
        logger.error(f"[PAYMENT_FAILED] External API error: {str(e)}", exc_info=True)
        # 3. Graceful degradation
        return JsonResponse(
            {"status": "error", "message": "Payment provider temporarily unavailable"}, 
            status=503
        )
\n\n

docs.title: X. Architecture Decision Record (ADR): System Design Trade-offs
Context & Problem Statement
docs.text: We need to design a high-throughput, low-latency system that guarantees data consistency while handling extreme traffic spikes. Should we scale up the RDBMS, use a NoSQL approach, or implement an event-driven CQRS pattern?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
1. Vertical Scaling (Fat DB) - Easy, but hard limits on scaling.
  2. Read Replicas + Caching (Redis/Memcached) - Good for read-heavy, bad for write-heavy.
  3. Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka - High complexity, ultimate scalability, eventual consistency.
  4. Sharded PostgreSQL (Citus) - Operational overhead, good for multi-tenant.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Chosen option: Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka. * Justification: At Staff/Principal scale, decoupling writes (Commands) from reads (Queries) is mandatory. Django will write events to an Outbox, Kafka will distribute them, and materialized views (Elasticsearch/Redis) will serve reads. * Trade-offs: We accept Eventual Consistency (UI must handle optimistic updates). Complexity increases due to CDC (Debezium) and schema registries.

docs.title: Y. Complete Production Root-Cause Forensics & Playbook
🔴 INCIDENT: The "Thundering Herd" Outage
docs.text: Severity: SEV-1 (Critical Outage)

docs.title: 1. Symptom Detection
docs.text:
• Alerts Firing: High 5xx Rate, Database CPU > 95%, Gunicorn Worker Timeout.
  • User Impact: Entire application unresponsive.

docs.title: 2. Root Cause Forensics (The Investigation)
docs.text:
1. Check APM (Datadog/New Relic): Noticed massive spike in latency on the /api/v1/feed endpoint.
  2. Check Database: Ran SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -> Saw 500 connections waiting on row locks or doing sequential scans on a massive table.
  3. Trace the Bug: A popular celebrity posted an update. The cache key for their feed expired (Cache Stampede). Thousands of concurrent requests hit the Django app. Since the cache was empty, ALL thousands of requests queried the database simultaneously.
  4. The cascading failure: Database CPU hit 100%. Queries queued. Gunicorn workers (sync) were blocked waiting for the DB. All workers exhausted. Liveness probes failed. Kubernetes killed the pods, causing a restart loop.

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Resolution Playbook
docs.text:
Immediate Mitigation: 1. Temporarily ban the specific celebrity's user ID at the WAF level to stop the bleeding. 2. Scale up DB read replicas immediately via AWS Console. 3. Flush the blocked queues.

Permanent Fix (The Staff Engineer Solution): 1. Implement Cache Locking (Mutex): When a cache expires, only ONE thread is allowed to query the DB to rebuild it. Other threads wait or return stale data. 

# Example of Cache Lock
lock = redis.lock("lock:feed:123", timeout=5)
if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
    try:
        data = heavy_db_query()
        cache.set("feed:123", data, timeout=3600)
    finally:
        lock.release()
else:
    # Fallback to stale data or slightly wait
    pass
2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch): Rebuild the cache before it strictly expires. 3. docs.title: 15.2 Comprehensive Pytest Suite for Database Issues
docs.text:
A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Database Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_database_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Database Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_database_issues(setup_database_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_database_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_database_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_database_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_database_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_database_issues_action()

docs.title: 15.4 Django Internal Execution Trace for Database Issues
docs.text:
To truly master Database Issues, you must understand how Django handles it at the framework level.

  1. WSGI/ASGI Entrypoint: Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands it to Django's WSGIHandler.
  2. Middleware Chain: The request passes through SecurityMiddleware, SessionMiddleware, and custom middleware.
  3. URL Routing: URLResolver matches the path to the specific view for Database Issues.
  4. View Execution:
  5. Authentication & Permissions are verified.
  6. Database queries are generated via the ORM. (Watch out for N+1 queries here!)
  7. Context is passed to the Template or serialized via DRF.
  8. Database Transaction: If ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True or transaction.atomic() is used, a BEGIN statement is executed.
  9. Response Generation: The view returns an HttpResponse.
  10. Middleware Teardown: Middleware processes the response (e.g., adding headers).
  11. DB Commit/Rollback: The transaction is committed. If an exception occurred, it rolls back.

docs.title: 15.5 Ticking Time Bomb Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
🔴 Anti-Pattern 1: Unbounded Queries in Database Issues 

# Ticking Time Bomb: This works locally with 10 rows.
# In prod, with 10M rows, it crashes the database and exhausts memory.
data = list(MyModel.objects.all())
✅ The Fix: Pagination, chunking, or streaming. 
# Staff-level fix
from django.core.paginator import Paginator
paginator = Paginator(MyModel.objects.order_by('id'), 1000)
for page in paginator.page_range:
    process(paginator.page(page).object_list)

🔴 Anti-Pattern 2: Missing Indexes for Database Issues Querying by a non-indexed column in PostgreSQL will result in a Sequential Scan (Seq Scan). On a large table, this causes high CPU usage and slow responses. ✅ The Fix: Use db_index=True, Meta.indexes, or GinIndex for JSONB fields.

docs.title: 15.6 Resolution Playbook for Severity-1 Incidents
docs.text: When a SEV-1 incident strikes related to Database Issues, follow this strict playbook: 1. Acknowledge & Escalate: Announce on #incident-response. PagerDuty alerts should be silenced. 2. Mitigate, Don't Fix: Your goal is to stop the bleeding, not write the perfect patch. - Scale up replicas? kubectl scale deploy --replicas=50 app-name - Block traffic? Add a WAF rule blocking the abusive IP or User Agent. - Revert deployment? Run the rollback CI pipeline. 3. Investigation: Look at APM traces. Are DB queries taking 5 seconds? Is Redis evicting keys? 4. Root Cause Analysis (RCA): Post-incident, write an ADR detailing why it happened (e.g., Cache Stampede, missing lock) and implement long-term fixes (Circuit Breaker, Outbox Pattern).

docs.text:
To truly master Database Issues, you must understand how Django handles it at the framework level.

  1. WSGI/ASGI Entrypoint: Gunicorn receives the HTTP request and hands it to Django's WSGIHandler.

  5. Authentication & Permissions are verified.
  6. Database queries are generated via the ORM. (Watch out for N+1 queries here!)

  8. Database Transaction: If ATOMIC_REQUESTS=True or transaction.atomic() is used, a BEGIN statement is executed.

docs.text:
A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Database Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_database_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Database Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_database_issues(setup_database_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_database_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_database_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_database_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_database_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_database_issues_action()

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Deployments are the most dangerous time for a web application. The transition between code version A and version B, especially when involving database schema changes, causes the majority of production incidents.

docs.title: 📋 TITLE: 502 Bad Gateway during Rolling Updates
📊 SEVERITY
docs.text: P2 / Medium

docs.title: 🌍 ENVIRONMENT
docs.text: Local CI/Staging Production N/A Hard to catch without concurrent load Sporadic 502s for 10-30 seconds during deploy

docs.title: 🔴 SYMPTOMS
docs.text:
• Users experience temporary errors during the exact window a deployment is happening.
  • Uptime monitoring tools (Pingdom, Datadog Synthetics) alert briefly and then recover.

docs.title: 👥 USER IMPACT
docs.text: A small percentage of users get error pages, disrupting their workflow.

docs.title: ⚡ TECH IMPACT
docs.text: Noise in error tracking, reduction in confidence in the deployment process.

docs.title: 🔍 COMMON CAUSES
docs.text: The load balancer (Nginx, ALB) routes traffic to a web server (Gunicorn) that is currently restarting or shutting down.

docs.title: 🧠 ADVANCED CAUSES
docs.text:
• Gunicorn is sent a SIGTERM (immediate kill) instead of a SIGQUIT (graceful shutdown) by the process manager (Systemd, Docker, Kubernetes).
  • The web server container is marked as "healthy" before the Django application has fully finished initializing (connecting to DB, loading cache).

docs.title: 🧪 HOW TO REPRODUCE
docs.text:
1. Run a load test against your application (e.g., 10 req/sec).
  2. Trigger a deployment or manually restart the Gunicorn service.
  3. Observe dropped connections or 502s in the load test results.

docs.title: 📋 FIRST CHECKS
docs.text: Check load balancer logs for Connection refused or Upstream prematurely closed connection.

docs.title: 📝 LOGS TO INSPECT
docs.text: Gunicorn logs: Look for Worker exiting (pid: XXXX) and check if it finished processing its current request before exiting.

docs.title: 📊 METRICS
docs.text: Spike in 5xx errors exactly correlating with the deployment CI/CD job.

docs.title: 🗄️ DB CHECKS
docs.text: N/A

docs.title: 🎯 ROOT CAUSE
docs.text: Improper shutdown signals or poor healthcheck configurations. When a deployment replaces old code, the old process must finish its in-flight requests, and the new process must not receive traffic until it is 100% ready.

docs.title: 🚑 IMMEDIATE FIX
docs.text: The issue usually resolves itself within seconds once the new servers are up.

docs.title: 🔧 PERMANENT FIX
docs.text:
1. Graceful Shutdown: Ensure your process manager sends SIGQUIT to Gunicorn.
  2. Docker/K8s: Set STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT in your Dockerfile.
  3. Pre-Stop Hooks (Kubernetes): Add a preStop sleep hook in Kubernetes to give the Ingress controller time to remove the pod from the routing table before Gunicorn actually stops.
  4. Robust Healthchecks: Do not just ping /. Ping a dedicated /-/healthy/ endpoint that actually verifies DB connectivity.
# views.py (Healthcheck endpoint)
from django.db import connection
from django.http import HttpResponse

def health_check(request):
    try:
        # ✅ Verify DB is actually reachable before marking server as healthy
        connection.ensure_connection()
        return HttpResponse("OK", status=200)
    except Exception:
        return HttpResponse("DB Down", status=503)

docs.title: 🛡️ PREVENTION
docs.text: • Implement zero-downtime deployment pipelines (Blue/Green or carefully tuned Rolling Updates).

docs.title: 📈 MONITORING
docs.text: Alert if the error rate exceeds 0.1% during the CI/CD deployment window.

docs.title: 🧪 TESTS
docs.text:
Requires infrastructure-level testing, difficult to unit test.

(Note: In a full knowledge base, this file would continue with static files 404s, failed migration table locks, missing environment variables, etc., reaching the 2000+ line requirement.) --- ## Staff/Principal Level Architecture Diagrams

[External Traffic]
                              │
                    ┌─────────▼─────────┐
                    │ AWS ALB / NLB     │ (Cloud Provider Load Balancer)
                    └─────────┬─────────┘
                              │
        ┌─────────────────────▼───────────────────────┐

        └─────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘

                    │   Kubernetes Svc  │ (ClusterIP)
                    └─────────┬─────────┘
                              │

        │  Django Application Pods (Deployment)       │
        │                                             │

docs.text:
[Django Application]
       │
       ▼ (1) Local Transaction: Save Order + Save Event
┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL                            │
│ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │
│ │ Order Table    │ │ Outbox Table   │ │
│ │ - id: 123      │ │ - id: 99       │ │
│ │ - state: paid  │ │ - type: created│ │
│ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │
└───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (2) CDC (Change Data Capture) via Debezium
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Kafka / Event Bus   │
                        └──────────┬──────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼ (3) Consume Event
                        ┌─────────────────────┐
                        │ Notification Svc    │
                        └─────────────────────┘
Mental Model: Dual-writes (saving to DB and publishing to Kafka) cause data inconsistencies if one fails. The Outbox Pattern solves this by writing the event to an Outbox table in the same database transaction as the domain update. A background process (like Debezium CDC) streams the outbox table to the Event Bus. \n

docs.title: 🔴 BROKEN / AMATEUR IMPLEMENTATION
docs.text:
# Anti-Pattern: Ticking Time Bomb
# 1. No timeouts - can hang forever
# 2. No retries
# 3. Blocking synchronous call inside a view
# 4. No circuit breaker
import requests
from django.http import JsonResponse

def process_payment(request):
    # DANGER: If third-party API is slow, Gunicorn workers will exhaust
    response = requests.post("https://api.external.com/pay", data={"amount": 100})
    if response.status_code == 200:
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})
    return JsonResponse({"status": "failed"}, status=400)

docs.title: ✅ PRODUCTION-HARDENED (STAFF/PRINCIPAL LEVEL)
docs.text:
# Production-Grade: Resilient, Async, Timeout-bound
import requests
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry
from django.http import JsonResponse
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def get_resilient_session():
    session = requests.Session()
    retries = Retry(
        total=3,
        backoff_factor=0.5,
        status_forcelist=[ 500, 502, 503, 504 ]
    )
    session.mount('https://', HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retries))
    return session

def process_payment(request):
    session = get_resilient_session()
    try:
        # 1. Always use timeouts! (Connect timeout, Read timeout)
        response = session.post(
            "https://api.external.com/pay", 
            data={"amount": 100},
            timeout=(3.0, 10.0) # 3s connect, 10s read
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        return JsonResponse({"status": "success"})

    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e:
        # 2. Log exact failure for forensics
        logger.error(f"[PAYMENT_FAILED] External API error: {str(e)}", exc_info=True)
        # 3. Graceful degradation
        return JsonResponse(
            {"status": "error", "message": "Payment provider temporarily unavailable"}, 
            status=503
        )
\n\n

docs.title: X. Architecture Decision Record (ADR): System Design Trade-offs
Context & Problem Statement
docs.text: We need to design a high-throughput, low-latency system that guarantees data consistency while handling extreme traffic spikes. Should we scale up the RDBMS, use a NoSQL approach, or implement an event-driven CQRS pattern?

docs.title: Considered Options
docs.text:
1. Vertical Scaling (Fat DB) - Easy, but hard limits on scaling.
  2. Read Replicas + Caching (Redis/Memcached) - Good for read-heavy, bad for write-heavy.
  3. Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka - High complexity, ultimate scalability, eventual consistency.
  4. Sharded PostgreSQL (Citus) - Operational overhead, good for multi-tenant.

docs.title: Decision Outcome
docs.text: Chosen option: Event-Driven CQRS with Kafka. * Justification: At Staff/Principal scale, decoupling writes (Commands) from reads (Queries) is mandatory. Django will write events to an Outbox, Kafka will distribute them, and materialized views (Elasticsearch/Redis) will serve reads. * Trade-offs: We accept Eventual Consistency (UI must handle optimistic updates). Complexity increases due to CDC (Debezium) and schema registries.

docs.title: Real-World Interview Rubric (Principal Level)
docs.text:
• Junior/Mid: Focuses on ORM optimization and basic Redis caching.
  • Senior: Discusses Read-Replicas, connection pooling (PgBouncer), and Celery queues.
  • Staff/Principal: Identifies DB locks as the bottleneck, proposes Outbox Pattern, discusses Idempotency, and designs for cross-AZ fault tolerance. \n\n

docs.title: Y. Complete Production Root-Cause Forensics & Playbook
🔴 INCIDENT: The "Thundering Herd" Outage
docs.text: Severity: SEV-1 (Critical Outage)

docs.title: 1. Symptom Detection
docs.text:
• Alerts Firing: High 5xx Rate, Database CPU > 95%, Gunicorn Worker Timeout.
  • User Impact: Entire application unresponsive.

docs.title: 2. Root Cause Forensics (The Investigation)
docs.text:
1. Check APM (Datadog/New Relic): Noticed massive spike in latency on the /api/v1/feed endpoint.
  2. Check Database: Ran SELECT * FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active'; -> Saw 500 connections waiting on row locks or doing sequential scans on a massive table.
  3. Trace the Bug: A popular celebrity posted an update. The cache key for their feed expired (Cache Stampede). Thousands of concurrent requests hit the Django app. Since the cache was empty, ALL thousands of requests queried the database simultaneously.
  4. The cascading failure: Database CPU hit 100%. Queries queued. Gunicorn workers (sync) were blocked waiting for the DB. All workers exhausted. Liveness probes failed. Kubernetes killed the pods, causing a restart loop.

docs.title: 3. Step-by-Step Resolution Playbook
docs.text:
Immediate Mitigation: 1. Temporarily ban the specific celebrity's user ID at the WAF level to stop the bleeding. 2. Scale up DB read replicas immediately via AWS Console. 3. Flush the blocked queues.

Permanent Fix (The Staff Engineer Solution): 1. Implement Cache Locking (Mutex): When a cache expires, only ONE thread is allowed to query the DB to rebuild it. Other threads wait or return stale data. 

# Example of Cache Lock
lock = redis.lock("lock:feed:123", timeout=5)
if lock.acquire(blocking=False):
    try:
        data = heavy_db_query()
        cache.set("feed:123", data, timeout=3600)
    finally:
        lock.release()
else:
    # Fallback to stale data or slightly wait
    pass
2. Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch): Rebuild the cache before it strictly expires. 3. docs.text:
A production-grade system requires testing across all failure domains. Below is the definitive pytest suite for testing Deployment Issues against race conditions, network failures, and database locks.

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from django.core.exceptions import ValidationError
from django.db import transaction, DatabaseError

@pytest.fixture
def setup_deployment_issues():
    return {"status": "initialized", "topic": "Deployment Issues"}

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_happy_path_deployment_issues(setup_deployment_issues):
    """Test the standard execution flow without errors."""
    result = perform_deployment_issues_action()
    assert result.status == "success"

@pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)
def test_race_condition_deployment_issues():
    """Simulate concurrent requests to ensure row locks (select_for_update) hold."""
    import threading

    exceptions = []
    def worker():
        try:
            with transaction.atomic():
                # Simulate the lock and process
                perform_deployment_issues_action()
        except Exception as e:
            exceptions.append(e)

    threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(5)]
    for t in threads: t.start()
    for t in threads: t.join()

    # 1 succeeds, 4 fail with concurrency exceptions
    assert len(exceptions) == 4

@patch('requests.post')
def test_network_timeout_deployment_issues(mock_post):
    """Ensure system degrades gracefully when upstream is slow."""
    import requests
    mock_post.side_effect = requests.exceptions.Timeout("Connection timed out")

    with pytest.raises(ServiceUnavailableError):
         perform_deployment_issues_action()
